Bending toward truth, we make our way slowly to Montoire. Well past due, my darling. Well past due, and still plenty of time ahead.
outputs.L3:
# The Turn Toward Plain Truth: Spring, Memory, and Mortality in the Poem's Design

With the arrival of spring, the poem undergoes a decisive shift in orientation—away from the ornamental gestures of poetic moralizing and toward something starker and more exacting. The speaker's demand that his song be "demoralized" is a striking inversion of expectation: rather than seeking to elevate or instruct through embellishment, he insists on stripping away the accretions of rhetorical polish that might obscure plain truth. This is not simply an aesthetic preference but an ethical stance, suggesting that the season's renewal calls for a corresponding renewal in language itself—one that resists the temptation to moralize and instead commits to unvarnished statement, even at the cost of conventional beauty.

This impulse toward directness finds concrete expression in the speaker's engagement with cartography. Poring over maps, he charts an imagined or remembered journey through specific French locations—the Brenne valley, Château-Renault, Montoire—each name carrying its own sedimented history and literary resonance. The act of consulting maps becomes a kind of ritual, grounding the poem's more abstract preoccupations in the particularity of place. Yet these are not merely geographical markers; they are palimpsests, layered with centuries of association that the speaker cannot help but summon even as he seeks plainness.

Indeed, the poem's landscape is inseparable from its populated history. The figure of Louise de la Vallière, mistress to Louis XIV, drifts through the text alongside the martial memory of Rooke and Butler's raid at Vigo Bay, and the enduring presence of Ronsard's verse. These references do not arrange themselves in tidy chronological sequence; instead, they blend and interpenetrate, allowing past and present to occupy the same imaginative space. The effect is a deliberate blurring of fact and legend, as though the accumulated weight of history has become indistinguishable from myth—each figure and event as much a literary inheritance as a historical occurrence.

This thematic instability is mirrored formally in the poem's syntax and diction, which increasingly fragment and collapse as the poem progresses. Sentences lose their expected shape; phrases arrive truncated or displaced. This formal disintegration is not a failure of craft but a deliberate strategy, enacting at the level of language the very difficulty the speaker faces in sustaining traditional poetic coherence amid the encroachments of age. The poem's structure becomes an analog for the speaker's own diminishing capacities, its broken syntax a formal correlative to the erosions of time upon both body and voice.

Threading through this fragmented terrain is the recurring refrain "high time," a phrase that insists on urgency, on the press of mortality against the dwindling present. Its repetition accumulates weight with each recurrence, marking time's relentless forward motion and the speaker's awareness of his own diminishing horizon. Yet this urgency is held in careful counterbalance against the tender, sustained address to "my love"—a phrase that offers warmth and continuity even as the poem's other elements insist on dissolution and endings. The tension between these two registers—the clipped, anxious "high time" and the enduring, affectionate "my love"—captures the poem's central paradox: a meditation on mortality that refuses to abandon intimacy, even as it acknowledges the truth that time is, indeed, running short.
outputs.L4:
# On Aging, Artifice, and the Grammar of Truth

The poem enacts, in real time, a crisis of poetic vocation. Its speaker is aging, and with that aging comes a suspicion of the very medium in which the poem is written—verse itself, with its inherited postures, its elevated diction, its centuries of borrowed grandeur. The poem's explicit desire "to demoralize my song" signals not a wish to write badly, but a wish to strip song of its moral posturing, its tendency to dress plain experience in ceremonial language. The speaker wants truth without the theatrical apparatus that usually accompanies poetic truth-telling.

This crisis is staged geographically. The poem moves through a real French landscape—the Brenne valley with its marshes and shallow lakes, the town of Château-Renault, the river town of Montoire—as though the physical act of travel might substitute for or ground the metaphysical travel of the poem's argument. These are not glamorous locations; they are provincial, workaday, the kind of places one passes through rather than visits. Their very ordinariness becomes part of the poem's argument against artifice: here is unglamorous France, unphotogenic France, the France that exists whether or not a poem notices it.

Yet the poem cannot simply abandon the literary and historical weight that clings to French landscape. Louise de la Vallière—Louis XIV's mistress, who ended her days in a convent, doing public penance for a love affair the whole court had witnessed—haunts the poem as a figure of love that curdled into spectacle, love made to perform itself for history. Ronsard, the great Renaissance poet of roses and mistresses and the carpe diem tradition, hovers as the ancestor of exactly the kind of song the speaker claims to want to escape—the beautifully wrought, courtly artifice of French lyric love poetry. Both figures represent what the poem is trying to move past: love and truth transformed into performance, into legend, into "song."

Formally, the poem embodies its own argument. As the speaker's resolve to strip away artifice intensifies, so does the poem's syntax fracture—clauses break off, connectives thin out, the diction grows plainer and more halting. The poem does not merely describe demoralized song; it becomes demoralized song, its grammar buckling under the weight of its own self-scrutiny. This formal collapse is not failure but enactment: the poem performs the very abandonment of poetic polish that its content calls for.

And yet the poem does not end in rubble. Having journeyed through fractured syntax, historical ghosts, and provincial towns, it arrives at something startlingly small: an aging partner takes off their glasses in order to read a map. That is all. No apostrophe to love, no grand statement about mortality survived or defeated—only this stooped, myopic, entirely unglamorous gesture, a small accommodation made necessary by aging eyes.

It is here, the poem suggests, that truth and love actually live—not in the elevated rhetoric of Ronsard's roses or the tragic legend of La Vallière, but in the humble adjustments two aging people make for each other and for the world: removing glasses, peering closer, figuring out together which road to take. The poem's real discovery is that authenticity does not require grandeur. It requires only attention to the stooped, myopic, entirely human moments that elevated song has always been too proud to notice.
outputs.L5:
# The Vernal Passage of Time

Spring arrives not as a single moment but as a gradual unveiling, a slow-motion revelation that time itself seems to soften during these weeks. The vernal season—from the Latin *vernalis*, meaning "of spring"—carries within its very name an ancient understanding that this period marks something more than mere calendar dates. It represents renewal, the turning of time's wheel toward growth and light.

There is something profound about how spring reorders our relationship with time. Winter's stillness gives way to movement; the frozen patience of dormant months breaks into sudden, insistent activity. Buds swell overnight, it seems. Birds return as if summoned by some internal clock more precise than any human invention. The vernal equinox itself stands as a testament to time's mathematical elegance—that precise moment when day and night achieve perfect balance, when the sun crosses the celestial equator and light begins its dominance over darkness.

Yet spring teaches us something paradoxical about time: that it can feel both urgent and unhurried simultaneously. We rush to notice each new bloom, each returning species, aware that these transitional weeks pass quickly into summer's fuller expression. At the same time, spring days seem to stretch, filled with a leisurely quality absent from winter's hurried darkness.

The ancients understood this vernal significance deeply, building festivals and rituals around this seasonal transition. They recognized that spring wasn't simply weather changing, but time itself demonstrating its cyclical nature—proof that endings give way to beginnings, that dormancy precedes flourishing.

Perhaps this is spring's greatest gift: reminding us that time, despite its relentless forward motion, moves in patterns we can trust. The vernal season returns, as it always has, carrying with it the promise that renewal is not just possible but inevitable, written into the very structure of how time unfolds upon the earth.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a free-verse poem that opens with the Pope quotation "stooped to truth and moralized his song" and follows an aging couple planning a springtime drive through the Loire valley towns of Château-Renault and Montoire.
counterfactuals.output:
*"Stooped to truth and moralized his song"*—
he read it aloud from the anthology,
glasses pushed up on his forehead,
the page catching afternoon light
the way pond water catches it,
brief and moving.

She was folding the map at the kitchen table,
the accordion of France resisting her,
Touraine creasing wrong again,
that soft crush of paper
like something folding inside the chest.

*Château-Renault first*, she said,
*then we can decide about lunch.*

He liked how she planned this way,
provisional, leaving room
for the day to answer back.
Forty-one years of that kind of talking.

Outside the window the forsythia
was doing what forsythia does,
too loud, too yellow, unembarrassed—
spring arriving like an opinion
nobody asked for.

He thought of Pope stooping,
the poet grown tired of pretty lying,
choosing instead the moral weight of things,
and he understood it differently now
than he had at twenty,
back when truth seemed like a destination
and not this—

this small brown town on the Loir,
the tanneries gone quiet,
the water still doing its slow argument
with the stone.

*Montoire after*, she said,
*there's that church with the frescoes,
the ones from the Crusades.*

He nodded, watching her hands
work the map's stubborn folds,
the age spots there like a further geography,
her wedding ring loose enough now
to turn with her breathing.

They would drive the D-roads,
windows down for the smell of rapeseed,
stopping wherever stopping seemed true—
not performing the picturesque
but suffering it, gladly,
the way old lovers suffer
each other's small deteriorations,
moralizing nothing,
just going.

The car would need gas.
He should check the oil.

Outside, the forsythia kept insisting,
kept being exactly what it was,
without apology,
the way, he thought,
a long life finally teaches you to be—
stooped, yes, stooped low
to whatever is true,
and singing anyway.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a fragmented, allusive poem mixing historical references (Vigo Bay, Rooke and Butler, Louise de la Vallière) with a present-day scene of a couple poring over road maps, using repeated phrases like "high time" as a refrain.
counterfactuals.output:
# Chart Room

High time we found the turning—
*here*, where the ink has bled into a river
that never existed, or existed once
near Vigo Bay, where Rooke and Butler
brought the galleons home in flame and silver,
treasure sunk before it reached the counting house.

You trace a road with one finger.
I trace the coastline of a war
fought for reasons no one now remembers—
was it trade? was it the queen's whim?
Louise de la Vallière wept into lace
for love that emptied out like tide,
and someone somewhere always weeps
for something spent too soon.

High time we found the turning.

The map folds wrong. It always folds wrong.
Somewhere under all this paper
a fleet is burning in a bay,
gold going down to feed the fish and silence,
and a woman in a court three centuries gone
is folding her hands the way you fold
this map, this stubborn accordion of roads,
this refusal to lie flat.

*Left,* you say. *No—here.*

High time. High time.

The past keeps interrupting like a static-crossed radio:
*Rooke pressed on. Butler held the line.*
The present says: *we're lost, we're lost,
the exit isn't marked, it never is.*

Louise retired to a convent afterward,
traded the king for God, one kind of vanishing
for a quieter one. I watch you
fold the map along its ancient creases,
white lines where the paper's memory
has given up on holding towns in place.

High time we found the turning.
High time the ships came home
or didn't. High time love became
a smaller, steadier flame—
not conquest, not surrender,
just this car, this argument,
this bay of paper we keep sailing
though the treasure's long since sunk
and the coastline never was
quite where we said it was.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

# Cueillez

*after Ronsard, after Shakespeare, after whatever this is*

**I.**

Somewhere between Blois and the last of the light
I am no longer certain which century
holds my hand—his roses or mine,
the vase already tipping, water
finding the tablecloth, a small country
of stain spreading where nothing
will ever be picked again.

*Cueillez, cueillez*—the old man said it
better, dying into French, into
the mouth of a girl who would be old
one evening, *au soir, à la chandelle*,
spinning wool, saying his name
and none of us there
to explain what he meant by *soon*.

**II.**

The train the train the train
doesn't stop it only slows
outside Amboise where the kings
are also compost now, and I
am rehearsing my grandmother's hands
in the shape of my own, the same
spots arriving like weather, like
mail from a country I don't
remember addressing.

Tomorrow and tomorrow and the small
pace of it, the town
creeping up through fog that isn't
fog exactly, more like the forgetting
that comes before forgetting, a rehearsal—

**III.**

—in the market at Amboise I bought
plums the color of held breath and could not
say *plum* in French, said instead
*prune*, said instead nothing, pointed,
the woman patient with my hands
which are becoming my mother's hands
which were becoming
someone's

I keep starting sentences
that arrive nowhere. Is this
what he meant, the old poet,
by *soon*, by *will be*, by
*you will remember me*
when I am
only

**IV.**

Roses this Roses that. The garden
at Chenonceau doesn't care
whose feet. The river underneath
still going wherever rivers go
when no one's asking them to mean something.

candle
guttering in a room
I no longer

tomorrow.
tomorrow, again,
and the fool
of me
still packing for a morning
that keeps arriving
already
over—

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a lyric poem for two elderly lovers planning a spring trip, blending literary epigraphs, French place names, and a self-aware commentary on the poem's own diction breaking down.
counterfactuals.output:
*"We loved, sir—used to love: that boat has sailed."*
—after Ronsard, badly translated by one of us

*"Grow old along with me"*—yes, well. We're trying.
—R. Browning, misquoted at breakfast

---

**I.**

You said *Arles*, and I heard *early*—
the ear going soft as an August peach,
still sweet, still catching the light wrong.
We are planning a trip the way old ships
are planned: with charts already half-erased,
with a captain who forgets the captain's name
but not the captain's face.

*(I wanted to write* still catching the light, full stop.
*The* wrong *crept in. Forgive it. Everything
now arrives with its own asterisk.)*

**II.**

Let's say Provence. Let's say the word *lavender*
and mean by it: forty years, a kitchen,
your hand finding my hand in the dark
like a man finding his glasses—
by touch, by faith, by the shape
of what he already loves.

We will go to Roussillon for the red earth,
to Sault for the fields not yet in flower,
to some village whose name I am already
losing, the way I lose the ends of sentences,
the way a poem loses its nerve
somewhere around the third stanza
and starts *explaining itself*—

*there. See it happening. The line just now
reached for a French word and found instead
the plain English of embarrassment.*

**III.**

Still. We'll go. We'll take the little roads
that go nowhere quickly, which suits us,
who take the same long way now to everything—
to the table, to the door, to the end
of what we meant to say
before the meaning wandered off
to look at something in the garden.

At Aix we'll sit where Cézanne sat
and fail, on purpose, to see the mountain right,
the way we've failed for decades
to see each other clearly—
which is its own kind of seeing,
the fond blur, the soft focus
love puts on an old face
so it still looks like the first one.

**IV.**

*Here the poem would like to say something final
about time, or light, or the Rhône going by
the way it always goes by, indifferent
and gold. It would like a strong last image—
a shutter, a window, a bell.

It has instead: your hand on the map,
tracing a route we may not live to take,
saying, quite simply, "There. That looks nice."

And that—not the bell, not the gold river—
that is the whole poem, breaking down
exactly where it should:
into a voice, an ordinary Tuesday,
two old people choosing, out of all the world,
one more small place to be together in.*
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

**Where Are My Glasses**

Where are my glasses. Where
the glasses are. The map
folds wrong, the map
folds the wrong way and you
say *here*, you say *no, here*—

*(Tourville turns his ships at Beachy Head,
the English line breaks like a sentence
nobody finishes)*

—hold it to the light. Hold
the light to it. My eyes
my eyes are not what
what they were. Louis
is not what he was, Versailles
still glittering, still
a mirror for a king who cannot
find his glasses either, who squints
at Colbert's ledgers, at the coastline
inked in France, in France, in
France that keeps receding—

I had them
a moment ago. A moment.
Ago is where the fleet
went down, is where the fleet
goes down each afternoon
in some textbook, some
footnote, some
forgotten strait between
d'Estrées and the wind—

Here. They're here. On the table.
On the table the whole time.

*(the wounded ship at anchor,
the wounded king in mourning black
for sons who die before the father,
1711, 1712, the dauphins
folding like a map that won't
fold back the way it came)*

Put them on. Now
read it to me. Read
the little roads, the little
towns too small for anyone
but us to care about—

*Nantes. Toulon. Brest.*

Say them slow. Say them
like a rosary of ports
where someone's navy
always was, always
is arriving, is
always just arriving—

I can see now. I can
see you now, still
holding the corner
down against the wind
that isn't there, the wind
that was there once, in sails,
in canvas, in the year
they burned the fleet at La Hogue
so the enemy could not
so no one could
say *this was ours*—

Fold it up. We know
the way. We've gone
this way before, before
before—

the glasses fog. Your hand
finds mine the way
a treaty finds
its signature: reluctant,
final, warm.
